claim: During aging and neuromuscular diseases, there is a progressive loss of skeletal muscle volume and function impacting mobility and quality of life.
source: During aging and neuromuscular diseases, there is a progressive loss of skeletal muscle volume and function impacting mobility and quality of life.
evidence: This is a general statement about aging and neuromuscular diseases that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Muscle loss is often associated with denervation and a loss of resident muscle stem cells (satellite cells or MuSCs).
source: Muscle loss is often associated with denervation and a loss of resident muscle stem cells (satellite cells or MuSCs); however, the relationship between MuSCs and innervation has not been established.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about muscle loss mechanisms.

claim: The relationship between MuSCs and innervation has not been established.
source: Muscle loss is often associated with denervation and a loss of resident muscle stem cells (satellite cells or MuSCs); however, the relationship between MuSCs and innervation has not been established.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in scientific knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: A subset of MuSCs specifically engraft in a position proximal to the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) in healthy young adult muscles.
source: We show that a subset of MuSCs specifically engraft in a position proximal to the neuromuscular junction (NMJ), the synapse between myofibers and motor neurons, in healthy young adult muscles.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In aging and in a mouse model of neuromuscular degeneration (Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase knockout – Sod1-/-), localized engraftment behavior of MuSCs was reduced.
source: In aging and in a mouse model of neuromuscular degeneration (Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase knockout – Sod1-/-), this localized engraftment behavior was reduced.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data comparing young, aged, and Sod1-/- mice.

claim: Genetic rescue of motor neurons in Sod1-/- mice reestablished integrity of the NMJ in a manner akin to young muscle.
source: Genetic rescue of motor neurons in Sod1-/- mice reestablished integrity of the NMJ in a manner akin to young muscle and partially restored MuSC ability to engraft into positions proximal to the NMJ.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from SynTgSod1-/- mice.

claim: Genetic rescue of motor neurons in Sod1-/- mice partially restored MuSC ability to engraft into positions proximal to the NMJ.
source: Genetic rescue of motor neurons in Sod1-/- mice reestablished integrity of the NMJ in a manner akin to young muscle and partially restored MuSC ability to engraft into positions proximal to the NMJ.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from SynTgSod1-/- mice.

claim: A subset of MuSCs are molecularly distinguishable from MuSCs responding to myofiber injury.
source: Using single cell RNA-sequencing of MuSCs isolated from aged muscle, we demonstrate that a subset of MuSCs are molecularly distinguishable from MuSCs responding to myofiber injury and share similarity to synaptic myonuclei.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by single cell RNA-sequencing data.

claim: A subset of MuSCs share similarity to synaptic myonuclei.
source: Using single cell RNA-sequencing of MuSCs isolated from aged muscle, we demonstrate that a subset of MuSCs are molecularly distinguishable from MuSCs responding to myofiber injury and share similarity to synaptic myonuclei.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by single cell RNA-sequencing data.

claim: Skeletal muscle atrophy and weakness are primary features of physical frailty and are common among the elderly and patients afflicted with neuromuscular disorders.
source: Skeletal muscle atrophy and weakness are primary features of physical frailty and are common among the elderly and patients afflicted with neuromuscular disorders (Marcell, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Marcell, 2003.

claim: Aging invokes decreases in number of MuSCs.
source: First, aging invokes decreases in number (Blau et al., 2015) and function (Schultz and Lipton, 1982) of a population of resident stem cells called satellite cells (Wang and Rudnicki, 2012; Shcherbina et al., 2020) or muscle stem cells (MuSCs) (Porpiglia et al., 2017), which are the principal source of myonuclei for muscle growth and regeneration (Yin et al., 2013; Almada and Wagers, 2016), contributing to muscle degeneration and sarcopenia.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Blau et al., 2015.

claim: Aging invokes decreases in function of MuSCs.
source: First, aging invokes decreases in number (Blau et al., 2015) and function (Schultz and Lipton, 1982) of a population of resident stem cells called satellite cells (Wang and Rudnicki, 2012; Shcherbina et al., 2020) or muscle stem cells (MuSCs) (Porpiglia et al., 2017), which are the principal source of myonuclei for muscle growth and regeneration (Yin et al., 2013; Almada and Wagers, 2016), contributing to muscle degeneration and sarcopenia.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schultz and Lipton, 1982.

claim: MuSCs are the principal source of myonuclei for muscle growth and regeneration.
source: First, aging invokes decreases in number (Blau et al., 2015) and function (Schultz and Lipton, 1982) of a population of resident stem cells called satellite cells (Wang and Rudnicki, 2012; Shcherbina et al., 2020) or muscle stem cells (MuSCs) (Porpiglia et al., 2017), which are the principal source of myonuclei for muscle growth and regeneration (Yin et al., 2013; Almada and Wagers, 2016), contributing to muscle degeneration and sarcopenia.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Yin et al., 2013 and Almada and Wagers, 2016.

claim: Impairments in innervation and synaptic integrity between motor neurons and myofibers become prevalent with aging.
source: Second, impairments in innervation and synaptic integrity (Ham et al., 2020) between motor neurons and myofibers (Shi et al., 2012) become prevalent with aging (Jang and Van Remmen, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ham et al., 2020, Shi et al., 2012, and Jang and Van Remmen, 2011.

claim: MuSCs have been shown to support the integrity of the NMJ by generating new synaptic myonuclei (SyM).
source: MuSCs have been shown to support the integrity of the NMJ by generating new synaptic myonuclei (SyM) (Liu et al., 2017), but how MuSCs sense and respond to innervation and how this behavior in old age remains poorly understood.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2017.

claim: How MuSCs sense and respond to innervation and how this behavior changes in old age remains poorly understood.
source: MuSCs have been shown to support the integrity of the NMJ by generating new synaptic myonuclei (SyM) (Liu et al., 2017), but how MuSCs sense and respond to innervation and how this behavior in old age remains poorly understood.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in scientific knowledge.

claim: Specific genetic depletion of MuSCs can accelerate aging-related NMJ deterioration through loss of SyM.
source: Recent studies have shown that specific genetic depletion of MuSCs can accelerate aging-related NMJ deterioration through loss of SyM (Liu et al., 2017) and reciprocally, MuSC depletion impairs the regeneration of NMJs after nerve injury (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2017.

claim: MuSC depletion impairs the regeneration of NMJs after nerve injury.
source: Recent studies have shown that specific genetic depletion of MuSCs can accelerate aging-related NMJ deterioration through loss of SyM (Liu et al., 2017) and reciprocally, MuSC depletion impairs the regeneration of NMJs after nerve injury (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2015.

claim: Disruption of innervation results in fusion of a subset of MuSC-derived progenitors adjacent to NMJs.
source: Herein, we assessed the response of MuSCs to functional and structural changes at NMJs. We demonstrate that disruption of innervation results in fusion of a subset of MuSC-derived progenitors adjacent to NMJs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: After NMJ perturbation in aged muscle, MuSCs migrate toward the NMJ but do not fuse as efficiently as in young adult mice.
source: We next show that after NMJ perturbation in aged muscle, MuSCs migrate toward the NMJ but do not fuse as efficiently as in young adult mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data comparing young and aged mice.

claim: Single cell gene expression analysis revealed a subset of MuSCs express transcripts associated with NMJs.
source: Single cell gene expression analysis revealed a subset of MuSCs express transcripts associated with NMJs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by single cell RNA-sequencing data.

claim: MuSCs expressing transcripts associated with NMJs are distinct from those that respond to muscle injury.
source: We next show that MuSCs expressing transcripts associated with NMJs are distinct from those that respond to muscle injury and are transcriptionally similar to SyM.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by single cell RNA-sequencing data.

claim: MuSCs expressing transcripts associated with NMJs are transcriptionally similar to SyM.
source: We next show that MuSCs expressing transcripts associated with NMJs are distinct from those that respond to muscle injury and are transcriptionally similar to SyM.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by single cell RNA-sequencing data.

claim: The subset of MuSCs expressing NMJ markers is also present in an orthogonal model of neurodegeneration (Sod1-/- mice).
source: We next demonstrate that this subset of MuSCs is also present in an orthogonal model of neurodegeneration (Sod1-/- mice).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from Sod1-/- mice.

claim: Genetic rescue of motor neurons by constitutive expression of SOD1 driven by the synapsin promotor in Sod1-/- mice (SynTgSod1-/-) attenuated NMJ degeneration.
source: Genetic rescue of motor neurons by constitutive expression of SOD1 driven by the synapsin promotor in Sod1-/- mice (SynTgSod1-/-) attenuated NMJ degeneration, decreased the presence of MuSC subsets expressing NMJ markers and partially restored the ability of MuSCs to contribute SyM after neuromuscular trauma.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from SynTgSod1-/- mice.

claim: Genetic rescue of motor neurons in SynTgSod1-/- mice decreased the presence of MuSC subsets expressing NMJ markers.
source: Genetic rescue of motor neurons by constitutive expression of SOD1 driven by the synapsin promotor in Sod1-/- mice (SynTgSod1-/-) attenuated NMJ degeneration, decreased the presence of MuSC subsets expressing NMJ markers and partially restored the ability of MuSCs to contribute SyM after neuromuscular trauma.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from SynTgSod1-/- mice.

claim: Genetic rescue of motor neurons in SynTgSod1-/- mice partially restored the ability of MuSCs to contribute SyM after neuromuscular trauma.
source: Genetic rescue of motor neurons by constitutive expression of SOD1 driven by the synapsin promotor in Sod1-/- mice (SynTgSod1-/-) attenuated NMJ degeneration, decreased the presence of MuSC subsets expressing NMJ markers and partially restored the ability of MuSCs to contribute SyM after neuromuscular trauma.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from SynTgSod1-/- mice.

claim: MuSCs respond to NMJ perturbations and motor neuron injury.
source: Collectively, these data reveal that MuSCs respond to NMJ perturbations and motor neuron injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Sciatic nerve transection (SNT) results in complete denervation and re-innervation 4–6 weeks after injury.
source: We contrasted acute and specific perturbation of motor neurons using sciatic nerve transection (SNT), which results in complete denervation and re-innervation 4–6 weeks after injury (Liu et al., 2017), with intramuscular injection of barium chloride (BaCl2) in extensor digitorum longus (EDL), a muscle primarily composed of type II fibers in mice.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2017.

claim: Only Pax7+ MuSCs are initially nGFP labeled along the length of isolated myofibers 5 days after tamoxifen administration, and devoid of precocious nGFP expression in myonuclei.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Liu et al., 2017), imaging myofibers 5 days after tamoxifen administration, only Pax7+ MuSCs are initially nGFP labeled along the length of isolated myofibers, and devoid of precocious nGFP expression in myonuclei (Figure 1b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2017 and by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: BaCl2-induced myofiber degeneration results in contribution of MuSC-derived progenitors and centrally located myonuclei along the entire length of the regenerated myofiber.
source: As expected, BaCl2-induced myofiber degeneration results in contribution of MuSC-derived progenitors and centrally located myonuclei along the entire length of the regenerated myofiber (Figure 1c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: 28 days after SNT during re-innervation, MuSC-derived myonuclei were confined at or near young NMJ myofiber regions (<250 μm from the NMJ).
source: In contrast, 28 days after SNT during re-innervation, MuSC-derived myonuclei (indicated by nGFP+) were confined at or near young NMJ myofiber regions (<250 μm from the NMJ, Figure 1c–d).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1c-d.

claim: Diffusion of molecules near the NMJ is limited to prevent synaptic transcription in myonuclei outside of the junctional area.
source: While we cannot discount that existing SyM incorporate nGFP after MuSC engraftment, diffusion of molecules near the NMJ is limited to prevent synaptic transcription in myonuclei outside of the junctional area (Schaeffer et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schaeffer et al., 2001.

claim: MuSCs are sensitive to NMJ disruptions, and in such contexts, fuse near NMJs.
source: Taken together, these results show that MuSCs are sensitive to NMJ disruptions, and in such contexts, fuse near NMJs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Approximately 20% of MuSCs are in the NMJ region (<250 μm from the NMJ) in young tibialis anterior muscles.
source: Myofibers were isolated from the periphery of young tibialis anterior (TA) muscles (to acquire type II fibers) with the myotendinous junctions attached at each end to ensure the entire length of the fiber was isolated, and MuSCs were observed along the length of the fiber with a percentage (~20%) that were in the NMJ region (<250 μm from the NMJ, Figure 2c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: There is a 30% decrease in the total number of MuSCs per myofiber in aged muscle compared to young muscle.
source: We utilized aged Pax7CreER/+-Rosa26TdTomato/+ TA muscles, administered tamoxifen as above, and observed a 30% decrease in the total number of MuSCs per myofiber in aged muscle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The percentage of MuSCs (~18%) proximal to the NMJs was similar in young and aged muscles.
source: Despite fewer total MuSCs per myofiber in aged muscle, the percentage of MuSCs (~18%) proximal to the NMJs was similar in young and aged muscles (Figure 2c–d) and young NMJs contained approximately the same number of SyM as aged NMJs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), when normalized to the total area of the endplate, which was slightly larger for aged muscles.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: Young NMJs contained approximately the same number of SyM as aged NMJs when normalized to the total area of the endplate.
source: Despite fewer total MuSCs per myofiber in aged muscle, the percentage of MuSCs (~18%) proximal to the NMJs was similar in young and aged muscles (Figure 2c–d) and young NMJs contained approximately the same number of SyM as aged NMJs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), when normalized to the total area of the endplate, which was slightly larger for aged muscles.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The endplate area was slightly larger for aged muscles compared to young muscles.
source: Despite fewer total MuSCs per myofiber in aged muscle, the percentage of MuSCs (~18%) proximal to the NMJs was similar in young and aged muscles (Figure 2c–d) and young NMJs contained approximately the same number of SyM as aged NMJs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), when normalized to the total area of the endplate, which was slightly larger for aged muscles.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Despite reductions in the total number of MuSCs with aging, the subset of MuSCs proximal to the NMJ is maintained.
source: These results suggest that despite reductions in the total number of MuSCs with aging, the subset of MuSCs proximal to the NMJ is maintained.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: After SNT, the post-synaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) were observed to fragment and exhibit diffuse staining for young and aged myofibers.
source: After SNT, the post-synaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) were observed to fragment and exhibit diffuse staining for young and aged myofibers.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Both young and aged MuSCs converged toward the NMJ post SNT and developed long projections.
source: Both young and aged MuSCs converged toward the NMJ post SNT (Figure 2c–d) and developed long projections, with a statistically significant increase in the number and volume of MuSCs for aged muscle that were in proximity to NMJs (Figure 2c–d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2c-d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a statistically significant increase in the number and volume of MuSCs for aged muscle that were in proximity to NMJs after SNT.
source: Both young and aged MuSCs converged toward the NMJ post SNT (Figure 2c–d) and developed long projections, with a statistically significant increase in the number and volume of MuSCs for aged muscle that were in proximity to NMJs (Figure 2c–d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2c-d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a statistically significant increase in the number of SyM for young muscle in response to SNT.
source: Contrasting the number of SyM 28 days after SNT revealed a statistically significant increase in the number of SyM for young muscle in response to the injury, but no change in the number of SyM post SNT for aged muscle (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: There was no change in the number of SyM post SNT for aged muscle.
source: Contrasting the number of SyM 28 days after SNT revealed a statistically significant increase in the number of SyM for young muscle in response to the injury, but no change in the number of SyM post SNT for aged muscle (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: MuSC depletion leads to loss of myonuclei proximal to young NMJs after SNT.
source: These results are consistent with previous reports whereby MuSC depletion leads to loss of myonuclei proximal to young NMJs after SNT (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2015.

claim: MuSCs are recruited to the NMJ as a result of acute denervation, but in aging, MuSCs do not contribute SyM as efficiently as in youth.
source: Coupling these results together suggest that MuSCs are recruited to the NMJ as a result of acute denervation, but in aging, MuSCs do not contribute SyM as efficiently as in youth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: A total of 34,930 single MuSC libraries were generated from young and aged WT FACS-sorted MuSCs.
source: Both young and aged WT FACS-sorted MuSCs (FSMs) from uninjured hind limb muscles were subjected to droplet-based single cell mRNA sequencing (scRNA-Seq) (Zheng et al., 2017) and a total of 34,930 single MuSC libraries were generated (12,057 young FSMs, 22,873 aged FSMs), yielding a mean of 5918 unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) and 1749 genes per cell after basic quality filtering.
evidence: This statement describes the experimental data generated in the study.

claim: The scRNA-Seq yielded a mean of 5918 unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) and 1749 genes per cell after basic quality filtering.
source: Both young and aged WT FACS-sorted MuSCs (FSMs) from uninjured hind limb muscles were subjected to droplet-based single cell mRNA sequencing (scRNA-Seq) (Zheng et al., 2017) and a total of 34,930 single MuSC libraries were generated (12,057 young FSMs, 22,873 aged FSMs), yielding a mean of 5918 unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) and 1749 genes per cell after basic quality filtering.
evidence: This statement describes the experimental data generated in the study.

claim: After filtering, data integration, and non-linear dimension reduction through UMAP clustering, seven clusters/cell type were observed.
source: After filtering, data integration, and non-linear dimension reduction through uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) clustering (Becht et al., 2019), seven clusters/cell type were observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–c) with a clear MuSC cluster that expressed myogenic regulatory factors (Pax7, Myf5, Myod1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b-c.

claim: A clear MuSC cluster was observed that expressed myogenic regulatory factors (Pax7, Myf5, Myod1).
source: After filtering, data integration, and non-linear dimension reduction through uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) clustering (Becht et al., 2019), seven clusters/cell type were observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–c) with a clear MuSC cluster that expressed myogenic regulatory factors (Pax7, Myf5, Myod1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Approximately 92% of young FSMs overlapped with the MuSC cluster.
source: Quantification of the number of cells that clustered with MuSCs compared with other clusters revealed that ~92% of young FSMs overlapped with the MuSC cluster (Figure 3c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Approximately 73% of aged FSMs overlapped with the MuSC cluster.
source: In contrast, ~73% of aged FSMs overlapped with the MuSC cluster (Figure 3c), and annotation of the clusters based on their unique gene expression profiles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–d) revealed that the largest non-MuSC cluster of FSMs expressed genes associated with the NMJ.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The largest non-MuSC cluster of aged FSMs expressed genes associated with the NMJ.
source: In contrast, ~73% of aged FSMs overlapped with the MuSC cluster (Figure 3c), and annotation of the clusters based on their unique gene expression profiles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–d) revealed that the largest non-MuSC cluster of FSMs expressed genes associated with the NMJ.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c-d.

claim: Re-clustering of cells in the NMJ-associated cluster showed a subset of Pax7+ cells within this cluster, which also expressed Myf5 and M-cadherin (Cdh15).
source: Re-clustering of cells in the NMJ-associated cluster showed a subset of Pax7+ cells within this cluster, which also expressed Myf5, a myogenic transcription factor, and M-cadherin (Cdh15, Figure 3d).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The subset of Pax7+ cells in the NMJ-associated cluster also expressed Rapsyn (Rapsn), a post-synaptically expressed protein that is essential for acetylcholine receptor (AChR, Chrna1) clustering and formation of NMJs.
source: This subset of cells also expressed Rapsyn (Rapsn), a post-synaptically expressed protein that is essential for acetylcholine receptor (AChR, Chrna1) clustering and formation of NMJs (Aare et al., 2016; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a and a citation to Aare et al., 2016.

claim: Other unique genes observed in the NMJ cluster were S100b, Cadm1, and Neuritin 1 (Nrn1).
source: Other unique genes observed in the NMJ cluster were S100b, a Ca2+ binding neurotrophic factor that induces neurite growth (Sorci et al., 2013), Cadm1 (Tanabe et al., 2013), a homophilic cell adhesion molecule that promotes synapse formation (Biederer et al., 2002) and interacts with synaptic proteins (Goda and Davis, 2003), and Neuritin 1 (Nrn1), a glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchored protein that is induced by neurotrophins (Naeve et al., 1997) and has previously been observed in MuSCs (Seale et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study and citations to Sorci et al., 2013, Tanabe et al., 2013, Biederer et al., 2002, Goda and Davis, 2003, Naeve et al., 1997, and Seale et al., 2004.

claim: S100b is a Ca2+ binding neurotrophic factor that induces neurite growth.
source: Other unique genes observed in the NMJ cluster were S100b, a Ca2+ binding neurotrophic factor that induces neurite growth (Sorci et al., 2013), Cadm1 (Tanabe et al., 2013), a homophilic cell adhesion molecule that promotes synapse formation (Biederer et al., 2002) and interacts with synaptic proteins (Goda and Davis, 2003), and Neuritin 1 (Nrn1), a glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchored protein that is induced by neurotrophins (Naeve et al., 1997) and has previously been observed in MuSCs (Seale et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sorci et al., 2013.

claim: Cadm1 is a homophilic cell adhesion molecule that promotes synapse formation and interacts with synaptic proteins.
source: Other unique genes observed in the NMJ cluster were S100b, a Ca2+ binding neurotrophic factor that induces neurite growth (Sorci et al., 2013), Cadm1 (Tanabe et al., 2013), a homophilic cell adhesion molecule that promotes synapse formation (Biederer et al., 2002) and interacts with synaptic proteins (Goda and Davis, 2003), and Neuritin 1 (Nrn1), a glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchored protein that is induced by neurotrophins (Naeve et al., 1997) and has previously been observed in MuSCs (Seale et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tanabe et al., 2013, Biederer et al., 2002, and Goda and Davis, 2003.

claim: Neuritin 1 (Nrn1) is a glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchored protein that is induced by neurotrophins and has previously been observed in MuSCs.
source: Other unique genes observed in the NMJ cluster were S100b, a Ca2+ binding neurotrophic factor that induces neurite growth (Sorci et al., 2013), Cadm1 (Tanabe et al., 2013), a homophilic cell adhesion molecule that promotes synapse formation (Biederer et al., 2002) and interacts with synaptic proteins (Goda and Davis, 2003), and Neuritin 1 (Nrn1), a glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchored protein that is induced by neurotrophins (Naeve et al., 1997) and has previously been observed in MuSCs (Seale et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Naeve et al., 1997 and Seale et al., 2004.

claim: Approximately 94% of young FSMs were Pax7+ based on immunostaining.
source: Immunostaining of young and aged FSMs with Pax7 showed that ~94% and ~93% were Pax7+, respectively (Figure 3c, labeled 'IF Young' and 'IF Aged').
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Approximately 93% of aged FSMs were Pax7+ based on immunostaining.
source: Immunostaining of young and aged FSMs with Pax7 showed that ~94% and ~93% were Pax7+, respectively (Figure 3c, labeled 'IF Young' and 'IF Aged').
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Young FSMs displayed a small fraction of Pax7+/S100β+ cells (~2%).
source: Young FSMs displayed a small fraction of Pax7+/S100β+ cells (~2%), which contrasted with the larger fraction of Pax7+/S100β+ (~16%) observed in aged FSMs, and these results were approximately consistent with the percentages identified through scRNA-Seq.
evidence: This statement is supported by data from immunostaining experiments.

claim: Aged FSMs displayed a larger fraction of Pax7+/S100β+ cells (~16%).
source: Young FSMs displayed a small fraction of Pax7+/S100β+ cells (~2%), which contrasted with the larger fraction of Pax7+/S100β+ (~16%) observed in aged FSMs, and these results were approximately consistent with the percentages identified through scRNA-Seq.
evidence: This statement is supported by data from immunostaining experiments.

claim: Comparison of Pax7+ cells with Pax7- cells in the NMJ cluster showed unique and shared expression profiles suggesting two different cell types.
source: Comparison of Pax7+ cells with Pax7- cells in the NMJ cluster showed unique and shared expression profiles suggesting two different cell types (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: There was a decrease in the number of Pax7 and Myod1 transcripts in aged MuSCs compared to young MuSCs.
source: We observed a decrease in the number of Pax7 and Myod1 transcripts in aged MuSCs and an increase in the number of Cadm1, Nrn1, Rapsn transcripts when compared to young MuSCs (Figure 3f) in strong concordance with our sequencing data (R=0.88, Figure 3—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: There was an increase in the number of Cadm1, Nrn1, Rapsn transcripts in aged MuSCs compared to young MuSCs.
source: We observed a decrease in the number of Pax7 and Myod1 transcripts in aged MuSCs and an increase in the number of Cadm1, Nrn1, Rapsn transcripts when compared to young MuSCs (Figure 3f) in strong concordance with our sequencing data (R=0.88, Figure 3—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: 2576 genes were differentially expressed between the NMJ-associated MuSCs and perisynaptic Schwann cells.
source: To further distinguish the sub-population of MuSCs from perisynaptic Schwann cells, the expression of the NMJ-associated MuSCs was contrasted with a pure population of perisynaptic Schwann cells Castro et al., 2020; 2576 genes were observed to be differentially expressed (Figure 3g, p_adj. < 0.05), and many genes upregulated in the NMJ-associated MuSCs were associated with inflammation (Mt1, Mt2, Tnfrsf12a, and Crlf1) and myogenic progenitors (Pax7, Myod1, Myf5), whereas upregulated genes in perisynaptic Schwann cells were associated with the synapse (Bche, Sema3c, Megf9) and perisynaptic Schwann cells surface receptors (Cd44).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Many genes upregulated in the NMJ-associated MuSCs were associated with inflammation (Mt1, Mt2, Tnfrsf12a, and Crlf1) and myogenic progenitors (Pax7, Myod1, Myf5).
source: To further distinguish the sub-population of MuSCs from perisynaptic Schwann cells, the expression of the NMJ-associated MuSCs was contrasted with a pure population of perisynaptic Schwann cells Castro et al., 2020; 2576 genes were observed to be differentially expressed (Figure 3g, p_adj. < 0.05), and many genes upregulated in the NMJ-associated MuSCs were associated with inflammation (Mt1, Mt2, Tnfrsf12a, and Crlf1) and myogenic progenitors (Pax7, Myod1, Myf5), whereas upregulated genes in perisynaptic Schwann cells were associated with the synapse (Bche, Sema3c, Megf9) and perisynaptic Schwann cells surface receptors (Cd44).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Upregulated genes in perisynaptic Schwann cells were associated with the synapse (Bche, Sema3c, Megf9) and perisynaptic Schwann cells surface receptors (Cd44).
source: To further distinguish the sub-population of MuSCs from perisynaptic Schwann cells, the expression of the NMJ-associated MuSCs was contrasted with a pure population of perisynaptic Schwann cells Castro et al., 2020; 2576 genes were observed to be differentially expressed (Figure 3g, p_adj. < 0.05), and many genes upregulated in the NMJ-associated MuSCs were associated with inflammation (Mt1, Mt2, Tnfrsf12a, and Crlf1) and myogenic progenitors (Pax7, Myod1, Myf5), whereas upregulated genes in perisynaptic Schwann cells were associated with the synapse (Bche, Sema3c, Megf9) and perisynaptic Schwann cells surface receptors (Cd44).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: A subset of MuSCs that express transcripts associated with the NMJ increase in aging and are distinct from perisynaptic Schwann cells.
source: Overall, these results show a subset of MuSCs that express transcripts associated with the NMJ increase in aging and are distinct from perisynaptic Schwann cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: scRNA-Seq recovered 14,329 cells after filtering from MuSCs isolated at 3 days and 7 days post BaCl2 injury.
source: MuSCs were purified with FACS at multiple time points (3 days, 7 dpi) and subjected to scRNA-Seq, which recovered 14,329 cells after filtering (7595 from 3 dpi and 6734 from 7 dpi, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This statement describes the experimental data generated in the study.

claim: UMAP dimension reduction and clustering revealed a continuum of MuSC states from uninjured to 3 dpi with activated cells from 7 dpi spanning an intermediate space.
source: UMAP dimension reduction and clustering revealed a continuum of MuSC states from uninjured to 3 dpi with activated cells from 7 dpi spanning an intermediate space (Figure 4b).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: A decrease in the percentage of FSMs that overlapped with the NMJ-associated cluster was observed for 3 and 7 dpi.
source: A decrease in the percentage of FSMs that overlapped with the NMJ-associated cluster was observed for 3 and 7 dpi, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Both the SyM and NMJ-associated MuSCs clustered together.
source: As expected, both the SyM and NMJ-associated MuSCs clustered together, and despite the MuSC heterogeneity before and after muscle injury, separation from the NMJ-associated cluster was observed for each of the time points.
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study.

claim: Despite the MuSC heterogeneity before and after muscle injury, separation from the NMJ-associated cluster was observed for each of the time points.
source: As expected, both the SyM and NMJ-associated MuSCs clustered together, and despite the MuSC heterogeneity before and after muscle injury, separation from the NMJ-associated cluster was observed for each of the time points.
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study.

claim: The decision to acquire a synaptic fate may occur over longer periods than 7 days, which is consistent with the time to stabilize the neuromuscular synapse during development (~1 month).
source: These results suggest that variations in MuSC fate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), and that the decision to acquire a synaptic fate may occur over longer periods than 7 days, which is consistent with the time to take to stabilize the neuromuscular synapse during development (~1 month) (Sanes and Lichtman, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by inference from the data and a citation to Sanes and Lichtman, 1999.

claim: scVelo-derived streams displayed trajectories from committed progenitors (MyoD1hi) isolated primarily at 3 dpi toward differentiating myoblasts (MyoGhi) that progressed toward myonuclei (Myh1hi or Myh4hi) or back toward the initial uninjured state.
source: scVelo (Bergen et al., 2020)-derived streams displayed trajectories from committed progenitors (MyoD1hi) isolated primarily at 3 dpi toward differentiating myoblasts (MyoGhi) that progressed toward myonuclei (Myh1hi or Myh4hi) or back toward the initial uninjured state (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The RNA velocity results were consistent with expression of canonical myogenic regulatory factors (Pax7, Myf5, Myod1, Myog) and previously observed regenerative dynamics.
source: These results were consistent with expression of canonical myogenic regulatory factors (Pax7, Myf5, Myod1, Myog) and previously observed regenerative dynamics5 (Dell'Orso et al., 2019), (Kimmel et al., 2020; Figure 4c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4c and citations to Dell'Orso et al., 2019 and Kimmel et al., 2020.

claim: Sod1-/- mice display age-accelerated NMJ degeneration and muscle loss early in life.
source: SOD1 is an antioxidant enzyme that scavenges superoxide (O2•–) radicals into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and protects from oxidative damage, and Sod1-/- mice (where Sod1 is globally knocked out) display age-accelerated NMJ degeneration and muscle loss early in life (Figure 5a; Jang et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jang et al., 2010.

claim: Degenerated NMJs with fragmented AChRs were observed in uninjured myofibers from Sod1-/- mice.
source: We observed degenerated NMJs in uninjured myofibers with fragmented AChRs (Figure 5b) and a decrease in the number of SyM after SNT (Figure 5c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: There was a decrease in the number of SyM after SNT in Sod1-/- mice.
source: We observed degenerated NMJs in uninjured myofibers with fragmented AChRs (Figure 5b) and a decrease in the number of SyM after SNT (Figure 5c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The decrease in SyM after SNT in Sod1-/- mice is consistent with an attenuation of MuSC ability to contribute SyM, as observed in aging.
source: This result is consistent with an attenuation of MuSC ability to contribute SyM, as observed in aging.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: scRNA-Seq of Sod1-/- FSMs recovered 6609 cells.
source: To glean further insights into molecular determinants that restrict MuSC fusion into SyM, MuSCs were isolated with FACS and profiled with scRNA-Seq recovering 6609 cells.
evidence: This statement describes the experimental data generated in the study.

claim: Similar to aged MuSCs, Sod1-/- FSMs contained fractions of cells that did not cluster with the primary MuSC cluster.
source: Similar to aged MuSCs, Sod1-/- FSMs contained fractions of cells that did not cluster with the primary MuSC cluster (Figure 5d, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–e).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-e.

claim: The largest non-MuSC cluster in Sod1-/- FSMs contained genes associated with NMJ function such as S100b.
source: The largest non-MuSC cluster contained genes associated with NMJ function such as S100b (Figure 5e), which was consistent with results from aged muscle.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Approximately 97% of Sod1-/- FSMs were Pax7+ based on immunostaining.
source: IF imaging of Pax7 and S100β in Sod1-/- FSMs revealed that ~97% were Pax7+ (Figure 5e, Figure 5—figure supplement 2a), ruling out contamination of other NMJ cell types through FACS.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Sod1-/- FSMs displayed increases in expression of genes that have been shown to perturb stem cell differentiation and become dysregulated with aging such as Igfbp5 and Ubb.
source: Sod1-/- FSMs also displayed increases in expression of a series of genes that have been shown to perturb stem cell differentiation and become dysregulated with aging (Oh et al., 2014) such as Igfbp5 (Soriano-Arroquia et al., 2016) and Ubb, a critical protein in the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (Ryu et al., 2014; Figure 5f).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5f and citations to Oh et al., 2014, Soriano-Arroquia et al., 2016, and Ryu et al., 2014.

claim: Degeneration of motor neurons and increases in oxidative stress from Sod1-/- results in modulation of MuSCs in a similar manner to aging, whereby MuSCs do not fuse as efficiently after nerve injury and remain in muscle expressing NMJ-associated transcripts.
source: Integrating these data shows that degeneration of motor neurons and increases in oxidative stress from Sod1-/- results in modulation of MuSCs in a similar manner to aging, whereby MuSCs do not fuse as efficiently after nerve injury and remain in muscle expressing NMJ-associated transcripts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Genetic rescue of motor neurons in SynTgSod1-/- mice prevents NMJ degeneration and muscle fiber denervation that is observed in Sod1-/- mice.
source: To determine if genetic rescue of motor neurons would revert the MuSC response observed in Sod1-/- to be more similar to that observed in young muscles, human Sod1 was specifically overexpressed only in motor neurons via the synapsin 1 promoter (Sakellariou et al., 2014) (SynTgSod1-/-). Previously, we showed that this rescue prevents NMJ degeneration and muscle fiber denervation that is observed in Sod1-/- mice (Su et al., 2021; Figure 5a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Su et al., 2021.

claim: Prior to SNT, AChRs in Sod1-/- myofibers were fragmented and contained fewer SyM than myofibers of SynTgSod1-/- mice that displayed canonical pretzel-like clusters.
source: Prior to SNT, AChRs in Sod1-/- myofibers were fragmented and contained fewer SyM than myofibers of SynTgSod1-/- mice that also displayed canonical pretzel-like clusters.
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study.

claim: After SNT, the number of SyM was increased for SynTgSod1-/- compared to Sod1-/-, but not statistically different from uninjured controls.
source: After SNT, the number of SyM was increased for SynTgSod1-/- compared to Sod1-/-, but not statistically different from uninjured controls (Figure 5c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Restoration of the NMJ partially augments the ability of MuSCs to contribute SyM.
source: These results suggest that restoration of the NMJ partially augments the ability of MuSCs to contribute SyM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: scRNA-Seq of SynTgSod1-/- FSMs recovered 11,790 cells.
source: To understand molecular changes in MuSCs from genetic rescue of motor neurons that may contribute to changes in MuSC ability to fuse into SyM, hind limb muscles from age-matched Sod1-/- and SynTgSod1-/- mice were harvested. MuSCs were extracted with FACS as above and profiled with scRNA-Seq, recovering 11,790 cells.
evidence: This statement describes the experimental data generated in the study.

claim: Similar to young FSMs, SynTgSod1-/- FSMs revealed a decrease in the percentage of FSMs that clustered with other cell types when compared to Sod1-/- FSMs.
source: Similar to young FSMs, SynTgSod1-/- FSMs revealed a decrease in the percentage of FSMs that clustered with other cell types (Figure 5d–e) when compared to Sod1-/- FSMs.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5d-e.

claim: Approximately 96% of SynTgSod1-/- FSMs were Pax7+ based on immunostaining.
source: IF imaging of Pax7 and S100β in SynTgSod1-/- FSMs revealed that ~96% were Pax7+ and displayed a comparable fraction of Pax7+/S100β+ cells as in youth (2%) (Figure 5e).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: SynTgSod1-/- FSMs displayed a comparable fraction of Pax7+/S100β+ cells as in youth (2%).
source: IF imaging of Pax7 and S100β in SynTgSod1-/- FSMs revealed that ~96% were Pax7+ and displayed a comparable fraction of Pax7+/S100β+ cells as in youth (2%) (Figure 5e).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Comparing the gene expression profiles of SynTgSod1-/- FSMs to Sod1-/- FSMs revealed increases in expression of Heyl, Fgfr1, and Foxo1, which have been associated with quiescence and healthy MuSCs.
source: Comparing the gene expression profiles of SynTgSod1-/- FSMs to Sod1-/- FSMs revealed increases in expression of Heyl, Fgfr1, and Foxo1, which have been associated with quiescence and healthy MuSCs (Figure 5f).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Prevention of NMJ degeneration attenuates the subset of MuSCs expressing transcripts associated with an NMJ and partially rescues MuSC ability to contribute new SyM.
source: Amalgamating these results shows that prevention of NMJ degeneration attenuates the subset of MuSCs expressing transcripts associated with an NMJ and partially rescues MuSC ability to contribute new SyM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Pax7+/S100β+ cells were rarely observed in uninjured S100β-GFP muscle.
source: Consistent with our results from young mice, Pax7+/S100β + cells were rarely observed in uninjured S100β-GFP muscle (Figure 6c), and very few S100β-GFP cells were detected outside of the synapse (Figure 6c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Very few S100β-GFP cells were detected outside of the synapse in uninjured S100β-GFP muscle.
source: Consistent with our results from young mice, Pax7+/S100β + cells were rarely observed in uninjured S100β-GFP muscle (Figure 6c), and very few S100β-GFP cells were detected outside of the synapse (Figure 6c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: S100β-GFP signals were observed outside of the synapse 28 days after SNT.
source: Next, we performed SNT on S100β-GFP muscles and extracted myofibers/myobundles 28 days after injury. As expected, we observed S100β-GFP signals outside of the synapse and a small percentage of Pax7+ / S100β+ cells in proximity to NMJs (Figure 6b–c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6b-c.

claim: A small percentage of Pax7+ / S100β+ cells were observed in proximity to NMJs 28 days after SNT.
source: Next, we performed SNT on S100β-GFP muscles and extracted myofibers/myobundles 28 days after injury. As expected, we observed S100β-GFP signals outside of the synapse and a small percentage of Pax7+ / S100β+ cells in proximity to NMJs (Figure 6b–c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6b-c.

claim: The increase in the number of S100β+ signals outside of nerve terminals was consistent with the known role of Schwann cells to guide regenerating axons.
source: The increase in the number of S100β+ signals outside of nerve terminals was consistent with the known role of Schwann cells to guide regenerating axons (Barik et al., 2016), (Son and Thompson, 1995) and suggests that changes in localized cellular signaling resulting from denervation may drive MuSCs to upregulate synaptic genes such as S100β.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Barik et al., 2016 and Son and Thompson, 1995.

claim: Changes in localized cellular signaling resulting from denervation may drive MuSCs to upregulate synaptic genes such as S100β.
source: The increase in the number of S100β+ signals outside of nerve terminals was consistent with the known role of Schwann cells to guide regenerating axons (Barik et al., 2016), (Son and Thompson, 1995) and suggests that changes in localized cellular signaling resulting from denervation may drive MuSCs to upregulate synaptic genes such as S100β.
evidence: This is a hypothesis suggested by the data.

claim: Increased S100β expression in primary myoblasts resulted in increases in reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: We confirmed increased S100β expression after introduction of sgRNAs compared to blank controls (Figure 6e, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), and consistent with previous observations (Sorci et al., 2004), detected increases in reactive oxygen species (ROS) (CellROX, Figure 6F) and apoptosis (TUNEL, Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6F and a citation to Sorci et al., 2004.

claim: Increased S100β expression in primary myoblasts resulted in increases in apoptosis.
source: We confirmed increased S100β expression after introduction of sgRNAs compared to blank controls (Figure 6e, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), and consistent with previous observations (Sorci et al., 2004), detected increases in reactive oxygen species (ROS) (CellROX, Figure 6F) and apoptosis (TUNEL, Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b and a citation to Sorci et al., 2004.

claim: Differentiation of myogenic progenitors that overexpressed S100β displayed reductions in fusion when compared to controls.
source: Differentiation of myogenic progenitors that overexpressed S100β displayed reductions in fusion when compared to controls, which was also in line with previous studies (Son and Thompson, 1995; Figure 6g, Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6g and Figure 6—figure supplement 1c and a citation to Son and Thompson, 1995.

claim: Denervation and chronic exposure to synaptic signals such as S100β may contribute to MuSC dysfunction observed in aging.
source: These results mimic aged and Sod1-/- MuSCs that displayed increased S100β and reduced fusion into SyM, suggesting that denervation and chronic exposure to synaptic signals such as S100β may contribute to MuSC dysfunction observed in aging.
evidence: This is a hypothesis suggested by the data.

claim: In young healthy muscle MuSCs support the NMJ through fusion into SyM.
source: Integrating these results permits construction of a model whereby in young healthy muscle MuSCs support the NMJ through fusion into SyM (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a model constructed from the data presented in the study.

claim: In aging, MuSC support of the NMJ is attenuated and contributes to NMJ degeneration through lack of ability to promote re-innervation.
source: However, in aging this support structure is attenuated and contributes to NMJ degeneration through lack of ability to promote re-innervation.
evidence: This is a model constructed from the data presented in the study.

claim: The neuromuscular synapse has traditionally been described to be controlled through bi-directional communication between motor neurons and SyM within muscle fibers.
source: The neuromuscular synapse has traditionally been described to be controlled through bi-directional communication between motor neurons and SyM within muscle fibers.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about the neuromuscular synapse.

claim: MuSCs integrate into the circuitry of the neuromuscular synapse and enact a localized retrograde response after denervation by engrafting into positions near the NMJ.
source: We show here that MuSCs integrate into this circuitry and enact a localized retrograde response after denervation by engrafting into positions near the NMJ.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: A subset of MuSCs are proximal to the NMJ across lifespan.
source: We also demonstrate that a subset of MuSCs are proximal to the NMJ across lifespan, and that the MuSC response to SNT is acute, but diminished with age and neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The MuSC response to SNT is acute, but diminished with age and neurodegeneration.
source: We also demonstrate that a subset of MuSCs are proximal to the NMJ across lifespan, and that the MuSC response to SNT is acute, but diminished with age and neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The inability of MuSCs to contribute SyM in aged and Sod1-/- muscle effectively leave behind a subset of progenitors expressing transcripts associated with the NMJ.
source: The inability of MuSCs to contribute SyM in aged and Sod1-/- muscle effectively leave behind a subset of progenitors expressing transcripts associated with the NMJ and are transcriptionally similar to SyM.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: MuSCs in denervated muscle fail to terminally differentiate.
source: These results are consistent with previous reports showing MuSCs in denervated muscle fail to terminally differentiate (Borisov et al., 2005a) and form smaller myotubes (Macpherson et al., 2011; Borisov et al., 2005b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Borisov et al., 2005a, Macpherson et al., 2011, and Borisov et al., 2005b.

claim: MuSCs in denervated muscle form smaller myotubes.
source: These results are consistent with previous reports showing MuSCs in denervated muscle fail to terminally differentiate (Borisov et al., 2005a) and form smaller myotubes (Macpherson et al., 2011; Borisov et al., 2005b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Macpherson et al., 2011 and Borisov et al., 2005b.

claim: The attenuated MuSC response to denervation in a Sod1-/- model can be improved by recovery of motor neurons.
source: We last show that the attenuated MuSC response to denervation in a Sod1-/- model can be improved by recovery of motor neurons.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Increases in denervation in advanced age may be in part driven or aggravated by reductions in MuSCs and inhibition to fuse into new SyM.
source: Summing these findings, we posit that MuSCs contribute to re-innervation and increases in denervation in advanced age may be in part driven or aggravated by reductions in MuSCs and inhibition to fuse into new SyM.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Schwann cells and glia secrete TGF-β after nerve injury to promote repair.
source: In addition to S100β, Schwann cells and glia secrete TGF-β (Fuentes-Medel et al., 2012; Feng and Ko, 2008) after nerve injury to promote repair (Jessen and Mirsky, 2019), and this signaling ligand inhibits myogenic fusion (Girardi et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fuentes-Medel et al., 2012, Feng and Ko, 2008, Jessen and Mirsky, 2019, and Girardi et al., 2021.

claim: TGF-β inhibits myogenic fusion.
source: In addition to S100β, Schwann cells and glia secrete TGF-β (Fuentes-Medel et al., 2012; Feng and Ko, 2008) after nerve injury to promote repair (Jessen and Mirsky, 2019), and this signaling ligand inhibits myogenic fusion (Girardi et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Girardi et al., 2021.

claim: Increases in expression of Igfbp5 in aged and Sod1-/- MuSCs are consistent with exposure to TGF-β.
source: In line with these observations, we detected increases in expression of Igfbp5 in aged and Sod1-/- MuSCs compared to young and SynTgSod1-/- MuSCs, which is increased after exposure to TGF-β (Kamanga-Sollo et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study and a citation to Kamanga-Sollo et al., 2005.

claim: Schwann cells and glia secrete multiple neurotrophic factors (glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, neurotrophin-3 and -4, nerve growth factor, and N-cadherin).
source: Conversely, Schwann cells and glia also secrete multiple neurotrophic factors (glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, neurotrophin-3 and -4, nerve growth factor, and N-cadherin), and these paracrine signaling factors have been shown to influence regenerative functions of MuSCs (Mousavi and Jasmin, 2006; Hicks et al., 2018) by signaling through the ERBB3 (Van Ho et al., 2011) and NGFR/p75 (Deponti et al., 2009) receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mousavi and Jasmin, 2006, Hicks et al., 2018, Van Ho et al., 2011, and Deponti et al., 2009.

claim: Neurotrophic factors secreted by Schwann cells and glia have been shown to influence regenerative functions of MuSCs by signaling through the ERBB3 and NGFR/p75 receptors.
source: Conversely, Schwann cells and glia also secrete multiple neurotrophic factors (glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, neurotrophin-3 and -4, nerve growth factor, and N-cadherin), and these paracrine signaling factors have been shown to influence regenerative functions of MuSCs (Mousavi and Jasmin, 2006; Hicks et al., 2018) by signaling through the ERBB3 (Van Ho et al., 2011) and NGFR/p75 (Deponti et al., 2009) receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mousavi and Jasmin, 2006, Hicks et al., 2018, Van Ho et al., 2011, and Deponti et al., 2009.

claim: Schwann cells and glia may shift in phenotype through aging or after persistent denervation from secretion of neurotrophic factors to a phenotype that inhibits fusion of MuSCs through secretion of TGF-β and S100β.
source: Thus, Schwann cells and glia may shift in phenotype through aging (Painter et al., 2014) or after persistent denervation from secretion of neurotrophic factors that positively signal to motor neurons and MuSCs (Li et al., 2019) to a phenotype that inhibits fusion of MuSCs through secretion of TGF-β and S100β.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings and citations to Painter et al., 2014 and Li et al., 2019.

claim: Reductions in MuSC number and attenuation of MuSC ability to fuse in aged muscle may contribute to lack of re-innervation and degenerative changes that occur at the muscle endplate.
source: While we cannot exclude that additional factors (Yang et al., 2021) and other cell types may also contribute to this process, our results suggest that reductions in MuSC number and attenuation of MuSC ability to fuse in aged muscle may contribute to lack of re-innervation and degenerative changes that occur at the muscle endplate (Li et al., 2011), (Valdez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings and citations to Yang et al., 2021, Li et al., 2011, and Valdez et al., 2010.

claim: Degeneration of the NMJ is a gradual process resulting from imbalances between denervation and new innervation.
source: Degeneration of the NMJ has been shown to be a gradual process (Martineau et al., 2018), resulting from imbalances between denervation and new innervation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Martineau et al., 2018.

claim: A critical factor that prevents axonal retraction and denervation is SyM that express AChRs and are anchored to the cytoskeleton by Rapsn.
source: A critical factor that prevents axonal retraction and denervation is SyM (Grady et al., 2005) that express AChRs and are anchored to the cytoskeleton by Rapsn (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Grady et al., 2005 and Li et al., 2018.

claim: The lack of engraftment from MuSCs may contribute to increased mobility of AChRs, reductions in number of SyM, and decreased ability to recruit detached axons and re-innervate.
source: Accordingly, the lack of engraftment from MuSCs may contribute to increased mobility of AChRs, reductions in number of SyM (Liu et al., 2017), and decreased ability to recruit detached axons and re-innervate (Aare et al., 2016; Verdú et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings and citations to Liu et al., 2017, Aare et al., 2016, and Verdú et al., 2000.

claim: The WNT signaling family plays a critical role in age-associated motor unit remodeling.
source: First, growing evidence (Henriquez et al., 2008) from in vivo and in vitro models suggests that the WNT signaling family (Budnik and Salinas, 2011) plays a critical role in age-associated motor unit remodeling (Koles and Budnik, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Henriquez et al., 2008, Budnik and Salinas, 2011, and Koles and Budnik, 2012.

claim: Non-canonical WNT signaling such as from Wnt7a in motoneurons has been observed to enhance AChR clustering and promote neurite outgrowth, synaptic assembly, as well as stimulate nerve terminal development and differentiation.
source: Non-canonical WNT signaling such as from Wnt7a in motoneurons has been observed to enhance AChR clustering and promote neurite outgrowth (Messéant et al., 2017), synaptic assembly, as well as stimulate nerve terminal development (Hall et al., 2000) and differentiation (Shen et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Messéant et al., 2017, Hall et al., 2000, and Shen et al., 2018.

claim: Wnt7a confers potent effects onto MuSCs and promotes engraftment as well as AChR expression.
source: Wnt7a also confers potent effects onto MuSCs (Le Grand et al., 2009) and promotes engraftment as well as AChR expression.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Le Grand et al., 2009.

claim: Aging has been observed to induce dysregulation of calcium (Ca2+) homeostasis.
source: Next, aging has been observed to induce dysregulation of calcium (Ca2+) homeostasis, and calcium-sensitive proteins such as S100β were observed to be upregulated in aged and Sod1-/- MuSCs.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about aging and calcium homeostasis.

claim: Ca2+ influx through mechano-sensitive cation channels or voltage-gated Ca2+ channels may play a role in dysregulated Ca2+ signaling in aged MuSCs and contribute to NMJ gene expression in MuSCs.
source: The mechanism of dysregulated Ca2+ signaling in aged MuSCs remains unresolved, but Ca2+ influx through mechano-sensitive cation channels or voltage-gated Ca2+ channels may play a role (Boers et al., 2018) and contribute to NMJ gene expression (Chen et al., 2011) in MuSCs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on citations to Boers et al., 2018 and Chen et al., 2011.

claim: Alterations in Ca2+ influx has been shown to modify MyoG ability to bind and activate targets.
source: In line with this and our observations of an attenuated response of MuSCs after denervation in aging, alterations in Ca2+ influx has been shown to modify MyoG ability to bind and activate targets (Tang et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2004.

claim: Ca2+-induced calmodulin-dependent protein kinase signaling has been observed to activate expression of genes associated with AChR clustering and NMJ formation such as Rapsn.
source: Additionally, Ca2+-induced calmodulin-dependent protein kinase signaling has been observed to activate expression of genes associated with AChR clustering and NMJ formation such as Rapsn (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2016.
